slot-title.what: The page title is the text shown on the browser tab, in history and in bookmarks. It also becomes the headline of a search result.
uses: Telling open tabs apart.
Naming a page in browser history and bookmarks.
Giving search engines a clear headline for the page.
avoid: Do not use it as the visible page heading; use the page's h1 for that.
Do not repeat the same title on every page.
practices: Put the part that is specific to the page first.
Keep it short enough to avoid being cut off in a tab.
Add the site name at the end.
Make every page's title unique.

slot-page-title.what: The page title is the single main heading at the top of a page. It tells people what the page is and gives screen readers a way to jump to the start.
uses: Naming a list, a record or a form.
Giving screen-reader users a clear starting point.
Confirming people landed where they meant to.
avoid: Do not use several top-level headings on one page; use lower heading levels for sections.
Do not use it for long sentences; use a subtitle.
practices: Use exactly one per page.
Keep it short and specific.
Match the label of the link people clicked to get there.
Use a real heading element, not styled plain text.

slot-page-subtitle.what: A page subtitle is one short line under the main heading. It explains what the page is for or what it covers.
uses: Explaining the scope of a list or report.
Adding context the title is too short to give.
Reassuring people they are in the right place.
avoid: Skip it when the title already says everything.
Do not use it for instructions that belong next to a form field.
practices: Write one sentence, not a paragraph.
Say something the title does not.
Use plain words, not jargon.
Keep the style the same on every page.

slot-page-actions.what: Page actions are the main buttons of a page, placed in a fixed spot near the heading. They hold the things a person can do with the whole page.
uses: Adding a new record from a list page.
Exporting or printing a report.
Editing the record shown on a detail page.
avoid: Do not put actions for a single row there; place them on the row.
Do not fill it with many equal buttons; group extras in a menu.
practices: Show one clear primary action.
Keep the same position on every page.
Start button labels with a verb.
Move rarely used actions into an overflow menu.

slot-breadcrumbs.what: Breadcrumbs are a row of links showing the pages above the current one. They show where you are and let you jump back up.
uses: Orienting people deep inside a site or app.
Going back to a parent list in one click.
Helping visitors who arrive from search on a nested page.
avoid: Do not use them on flat sites with only one level; use plain navigation.
Do not use them as the main way to move around.
practices: Show the path from the top level to the current page.
Make the last item plain text, not a link.
Keep labels short and match page titles.
Place them above the page title.

slot-content.what: The content region is the main area of a page where its own material goes. Everything around it, such as the header and navigation, stays the same from page to page.
uses: Holding the main text, forms or tables of a page.
Keeping a consistent frame around changing content.
Letting screen readers skip straight to the main part.
avoid: Do not put site-wide navigation or footers inside it.
Do not make several competing main regions on one page.
practices: Use one main region per page.
Mark it so skip links can reach it.
Structure it with clear headings and spacing.
Leave the surrounding frame untouched.

slot-scripts.what: A scripts region holds the JavaScript files a page loads, placed at the end of the page. This lets the visible content appear first.
uses: Loading site-wide behaviour such as menus.
Adding analytics or a shared library.
Keeping all script tags in one predictable place.
avoid: Do not load scripts for one page on every page; load them only where needed.
Do not put code the page needs before it renders at the end.
practices: Load scripts at the end or with defer.
Include only what the page uses.
Keep scripts in one place.
Make sure the page still works with scripts that fail to load.

slot-head.what: The head of a page holds information for the browser that is not shown on screen: stylesheets, the icon, the title and meta tags.
uses: Linking stylesheets and fonts.
Setting the page icon and character set.
Adding meta tags for phones and search engines.
avoid: Do not put visible content in it; use the body.
Do not copy the head into every page by hand; share it.
practices: Set the character encoding first.
Include the viewport meta tag for phones.
Keep it in one shared place.
Load only the styles the page needs.

slot-body-class.what: A body class is a name added to the page's body element so styles can target one kind of page. It changes a page's look without touching shared code.
uses: Giving a single page its own layout tweak.
Marking the type of page, such as an app or a report.
Switching a page to a full-width mode.
avoid: Do not use it to restyle individual components; style those directly.
Do not use it to store state that scripts depend on.
practices: Use short, descriptive names.
Keep the classes the layout already needs.
Scope styles with the class instead of overriding globally.
Remove unused classes.

slot-sidebar.what: A sidebar is a vertical panel at the side of a page. It usually holds the main navigation and can collapse to save room.
uses: Showing the main sections of an application.
Keeping navigation visible while content scrolls.
Docs sites with a long list of pages.
avoid: Avoid it on short flows such as sign-up or checkout; use a simple page.
Avoid it for sites with only a few links; use a top bar.
practices: Keep the order of items the same everywhere.
Mark the current page.
Let it collapse on small screens.
Limit the number of top-level items.

slot-top-bar.what: A top bar is a strip across the top of every page. It holds the brand, main links and the person's own controls such as search or account.
uses: Showing the logo and a link home.
Offering search, notifications and the account menu.
Giving public sites their main navigation.
avoid: Do not crowd it with many links; move extras to a sidebar or menu.
Do not hide it on every scroll when people need quick access.
practices: Keep it in the same place on every page.
Put the logo on the left and personal tools on the right.
Keep the height small.
Collapse links into a menu on phones.

slot-brand.what: The brand area shows the logo or name of a product or company. It usually links back to the home page.
uses: Confirming whose site this is.
Giving a one-click way back home.
Repeating identity across all pages.
avoid: Do not use large logos that push content down; keep them compact.
Do not make it the only way to reach home on small screens without a label.
practices: Place it in the same corner on every page.
Link it to the home page.
Give the logo image useful alternative text.
Use a version that stays readable on small screens.

slot-sidebar-extra.what: A sidebar extra area is space under the main navigation for secondary items, such as a site switcher, a usage meter or a help link.
uses: Switching between sites or workspaces.
Showing plan or storage usage.
Linking to help and support.
avoid: Do not put main navigation here; keep it in the navigation list.
Do not add long content; it crowds the navigation.
practices: Keep it short.
Group related items together.
Put the most useful item first.
Make sure it works when the sidebar is narrow.

slot-sidebar-nav.what: Sidebar navigation is a list of links to the main sections of an app, usually grouped under short labels. It stays on screen as you move around.
uses: Moving between the main areas of an application.
Showing where you are right now.
Grouping many pages into clear sections.
avoid: Avoid it for a handful of links; use a top bar.
Avoid deep nesting; use breadcrumbs or tabs for lower levels.
practices: Group related links under clear labels.
Mark the current page.
Use short, plain item names.
Keep the order stable between visits.

slot-filter-panel.what: A filter panel is a set of controls for narrowing a list, often in a drawer or side panel. People pick values and the list updates.
uses: Narrowing a long list by status, date or owner.
Combining several filters at once.
Keeping the list visible while filters stay out of the way.
avoid: Avoid it for one or two simple filters; show them above the list.
Avoid it for finding by name; use a search box.
practices: Open it from a clearly labelled Filters button.
Show which filters are active.
Offer a way to clear all filters.
Apply filters without losing the person's place.

slot-body.what: The body of a page is everything people see in the browser window. A layout fills it with the frame around the page's own content.
uses: Defining the overall structure of a page type.
Building a new kind of layout.
Placing the skip link, main area and dialogs.
avoid: Do not replace it on ordinary pages; fill the content area instead.
Do not put hidden tracking content in it.
practices: Use proper landmark regions such as header, main and footer.
Keep one main region.
Place a skip link first.
Keep structure the same across pages.

slot-modal.what: A modal region is the place in a page where dialogs and drawers are kept. They appear above everything else when opened.
uses: Holding confirmation dialogs.
Holding side drawers with forms or details.
Keeping overlays out of the page's normal flow.
avoid: Do not use a dialog for content people need to compare with the page; use a panel.
Do not open dialogs automatically on load.
practices: Give each dialog a title.
Move focus into it when it opens.
Let Escape close it.
Return focus to the button that opened it.

slot-footer.what: A footer is the area at the end of a page. It holds links people expect to find last, such as legal notices, contact details and help.
uses: Linking to terms, privacy and contact pages.
Showing the app version or copyright.
Repeating key links for people who reach the bottom.
avoid: Do not hide essential actions there; people may never scroll that far.
Do not overload it with every site link.
practices: Keep it the same on every page.
Group links under short headings.
Keep text small but readable.
Include only links people need.

slot-extra-head.what: An extra head area lets one page add its own items to the head: a stylesheet, meta tags or preloaded files, without copying the shared head.
uses: Adding a page-specific stylesheet.
Setting a page's social sharing tags.
Telling search engines not to index one page.
avoid: Do not use it for content every page needs; add that to the shared head.
Do not use it to restyle the whole site.
practices: Add only what this page needs.
Keep additions small.
Do not repeat tags the shared head already sets.
Test that the page still loads fast.

slot-extra-scripts.what: An extra scripts area lets one page load its own JavaScript after the site-wide scripts. Other pages stay lighter because they skip it.
uses: Loading a chart library on a report page.
Adding behaviour for one form.
Running a small page-specific script.
avoid: Do not use it for scripts every page needs; load those site-wide.
Do not use it for behaviour a plain HTML feature already gives.
practices: Load with defer.
Include only what the page uses.
Keep files small.
Make sure the page still works if the script fails.

slot-theme-bootstrap.what: A theme bootstrap is a tiny script that runs early and applies the reader's saved light or dark choice before the page is drawn, so there is no flash of the wrong colours.
uses: Remembering a dark theme between visits.
Avoiding a white flash on page load.
Applying a theme set by the system.
avoid: Do not use it if the site has only one theme; it is not needed.
Do not make it large; slow code defeats the purpose.
practices: Run it before the page is drawn.
Keep it very small.
Fall back to the system preference.
Save the choice in a place the script can read.

slot-list-actions.what: List actions are the buttons at the top of a list page, such as adding a record, exporting or running bulk tools.
uses: Adding a new item to a list.
Exporting the list to a file.
Starting actions on many selected rows.
avoid: Do not put actions for one row here; keep them on that row.
Do not show many equal buttons; keep one primary action.
practices: Put the main add button first.
Start labels with a verb and name the item.
Keep the position the same on every list.
Group less common actions in a menu.

slot-detail-actions.what: Detail actions are the buttons on the page of a single record, such as edit, duplicate or delete. They sit together near the record's title.
uses: Editing the record being viewed.
Deleting or archiving the record.
Running other one-off actions such as export.
avoid: Do not place delete beside the main action without separation; set it apart.
Do not hide Edit in a menu on a detail page.
practices: Put Edit first and Delete last.
Make Delete look quieter and ask for confirmation.
Use clear verb labels.
Keep the same positions on every record.

schedule-row.what: A schedule row is one line of a repeating timetable: a day plus a start and end time. Several rows together describe opening hours or working hours.
uses: Setting opening hours for a shop or service.
Defining working hours for staff.
Setting recurring availability for bookings.
avoid: Do not use it for one-off dates; use an exception or a date picker.
Do not use it for a single time; use one time field.
practices: Allow more than one row per day for split shifts.
Use 24-hour times or label AM and PM.
Check that end is after start.
Label each field for screen readers.

add-row-button.what: An add-row button adds one more empty set of fields to a repeating group, such as another time slot or another phone number.
uses: Adding a time span to a schedule.
Adding another reminder, address or contact.
Building lists of unknown length in a form.
avoid: Avoid it when the number of rows is small and fixed; show them all.
Avoid it for picking from known options; use checkboxes.
practices: Label it with what it adds, such as Add hours.
Place it right below the last row.
Move focus to the new row.
Hide or disable it at the limit and say why.

remove-row-button.what: A remove-row button deletes one row from a repeating group of fields. It is usually a small icon button at the end of the row.
uses: Deleting a time span from a schedule.
Removing an extra contact or reminder.
Trimming any repeated set of fields.
avoid: Do not use it for deleting important records; use a delete button with confirmation.
Do not use it for the only required row.
practices: Give it a name saying which row it removes.
Move focus to a sensible place afterwards.
Announce the removal to screen readers.
Make it big enough to tap.

availability-legend.what: An availability legend is a small key that explains the marks used in a calendar or booking grid, such as free, busy and unavailable.
uses: Explaining colours and patterns in a scheduler.
Helping people read booking grids.
Explaining resource availability rows.
avoid: Skip it when marks are labelled directly with words.
Do not rely on colour alone; use text or shapes as well.
practices: Place it near the grid it explains.
Use the same marks as the grid.
Pair colour with a word or pattern.
Keep the list short.

exception-entry.what: An exception entry records a single day that differs from the usual schedule, such as a holiday closure or special opening hours, with the reason.
uses: Marking public holidays as closed.
Setting special hours for an event day.
Listing maintenance days.
avoid: Do not use it for regular weekly changes; edit the weekly schedule.
Do not use it for long absences; use a date range.
practices: Show the date clearly.
Give the reason in plain words.
Sort entries by date.
Let people edit or remove an entry.

time-off-entry.what: A time-off entry is a row describing a person's absence: who is away, on which dates, for what reason and whether it is approved.
uses: Listing holiday requests for a team.
Showing who is away on a team calendar.
Reviewing requests waiting for approval.
avoid: Do not use it for a single-day opening change; use an exception.
Do not use it for tasks or meetings; use calendar events.
practices: Show name, dates and length together.
Show the status in words, not colour alone.
Format dates the way people read them.
Sort by start date.

booking-slot.what: A booking slot is a button showing one time someone can book, with its state: free, limited, full or chosen.
uses: Choosing an appointment time.
Booking a table, room or class.
Showing which times are still open.
avoid: Avoid it for picking a date far ahead; use a calendar.
Avoid it when times are free-form; use a time field.
practices: Show all times for a day at once.
Show full slots as unavailable rather than hiding them.
Make buttons big enough to tap.
Show the chosen slot clearly.

conflict-warning.what: A conflict warning is a message that tells someone their plan clashes with something else, such as a double booking, and how to fix it.
uses: Warning about a double-booked person or room.
Flagging a shift that overlaps another.
Alerting someone about a clash before saving.
avoid: Do not use it for ordinary errors; use field error messages.
Do not show it if there is no real clash.
practices: Say exactly what clashes.
Link to the other item.
Offer clear ways to fix it.
Allow saving anyway only when it is safe.

overlap-warning.what: An overlap warning is a short message next to a schedule row saying its times overlap another row, so the person can fix it right there.
uses: Checking opening hours rows while editing.
Catching overlapping shifts.
Validating time ranges in forms.
avoid: Do not wait until the form is submitted to report it.
Do not use it for unrelated errors; use normal field messages.
practices: Show it next to the row it affects.
Name the other row it overlaps.
Tell people how to fix it.
Connect it to the fields for screen readers.

working-hours-label.what: A working-hours label is a short line saying whether a place is open right now and when that next changes, often with a small status dot.
uses: Showing if a shop or support desk is open.
Telling visitors when to call.
Showing availability on a contact page.
avoid: Do not use it when hours are only approximate; list the hours instead.
Do not show it without handling holidays and time zones.
practices: Use words as well as a coloured dot.
Show the next change, such as closes at 18:00.
Use the place's own time zone.
Keep it up to date.

marketing-hero.what: A hero is the large opening section at the top of a landing page. It states the main benefit and gives one clear next step.
uses: Introducing a product on a home page.
Starting a campaign or launch page.
Pointing visitors to sign up or learn more.
avoid: Do not use it on inner pages; use a plain page heading.
Do not use it in an application screen.
practices: Write a headline that states the benefit.
Offer one main button.
Add a few real proof points.
Use an image that shows the product.

feature-grid.what: A feature grid is a set of small blocks, each with an icon, a short title and a sentence. Together they summarise what a product offers.
uses: Summarising product benefits on a landing page.
Highlighting new releases.
Giving an overview of a service.
avoid: Do not use it for step-by-step instructions; use a numbered list.
Do not use it for dense detail; link to a full page.
practices: Use three to six features.
Keep text lengths similar.
Lead with the benefit in each title.
Use icons that match the meaning.

token-panel.what: A design-token panel lets people change brand values such as colours and see the effect on sample components straight away.
uses: Trying brand colours before applying them.
Documenting how a design system is customised.
Branding settings pages for admins.
avoid: Do not use it for ordinary user preferences; use settings forms.
Do not use it for production changes without a save step.
practices: Preview on real components.
Update the preview instantly.
Show contrast results next to each colour.
Offer a way to reset.

code-samples.what: A code samples block shows the same example in several languages or tools, usually as tabs. Readers pick their own and copy it.
uses: Showing API requests in different languages.
Giving install steps for several platforms.
Comparing framework versions of an example.
avoid: Do not use it for a single language; show one code block.
Do not use it for long programs; link to a repository.
practices: Remember the language the reader chose.
Add a copy button to each block.
Keep examples equivalent.
Keep samples short and runnable.

docs-page-header.what: A documentation page header sits at the top of a docs page. It gives the trail, title, a short introduction and details like status or version.
uses: Starting every page of a documentation site.
Showing whether a feature is stable or in beta.
Telling readers what a page covers.
avoid: Do not use it on marketing pages; use a hero.
Do not make the intro long; link to details.
practices: Put the answer to what this page is first.
Keep the intro to one or two sentences.
Show status in words as well as colour.
Use the same layout everywhere.

docs-sidebar.what: A docs sidebar is the navigation column of a documentation site. It lists pages in groups, often with a search box to filter them.
uses: Browsing the pages of a large docs site.
Finding a page by typing part of its name.
Showing where the current page sits.
avoid: Avoid it for a very small site; use a short top menu.
Avoid it as a search replacement across all content.
practices: Group pages under clear headings.
Open the group of the current page.
Offer a filter box.
Turn it into a drawer on phones.

table-of-contents.what: A table of contents lists the sections of a long page as links. It shows what the page covers and lets people jump to a section.
uses: Guiding readers through long articles.
Navigating documentation and guides.
Finding a heading in release notes.
avoid: Avoid it on short pages with few sections.
Do not use it to move between pages; use navigation.
practices: Use section titles as labels.
Highlight the section being read.
Keep it visible while scrolling on wide screens.
List top-level headings only.

recording-player.what: A recording player plays a saved video and shows marks on a timeline for important moments. A list of events lets people jump straight to each one.
uses: Reviewing footage after an alert.
Checking incidents in recorded clips.
Finding key moments in a long recording.
avoid: Do not use it for live video; use a live view.
Do not use it for short decorative clips; use a plain video element.
practices: Use the browser's own video controls.
Label timeline marks with time and event.
Add captions when the clip has speech.
Show a loading message while it prepares.

live-stream-panel.what: A live stream panel shows live video next to its state and current numbers, so one glance tells the whole story.
uses: Monitoring cameras or feeds.
Watching a live event with live stats.
Building a monitoring wall.
avoid: Do not use it for saved clips; use a recording player.
Do not autoplay sound; it surprises people.
practices: Label the stream as live.
Show clearly when the stream is offline.
Keep counts close to the picture.
Offer pause and full-screen controls.

photo-post.what: A photo post is a shared picture with the author, time, actions and caption. It is the building block of feeds and team updates.
uses: Sharing snapshots in a team feed.
Showing community posts.
Posting progress photos with comments.
avoid: Do not use it for a collection of many images; use a gallery.
Do not use it for official documents; use a file list.
practices: Show who posted and when.
Add alternative text to the photo.
Keep the caption near the photo.
Make like and comment buttons easy to tap.

image-gallery.what: An image gallery shows one large image with a row of small previews below. Clicking a preview swaps the large image.
uses: Showing product photos.
Comparing before and after pictures.
Browsing several snapshots of one event.
avoid: Avoid it for a single image; just show the image.
Avoid it for hundreds of images; use a paged grid.
practices: Give every image useful alternative text.
Show which image is selected and how many exist.
Make previews big enough to tap.
Load previews at small sizes.
